name: THE JUDGE, THE JURY, AND THE LAWYERS
safetyNote: Nothing here is legal advice, and nothing here tells you what to do. It tells you who does what in a courtroom. Six of these questions say "in Michigan" because those rules are Michigan's own choice and other states do it differently. The rest are the same everywhere in the country.

questions.q: A jury in Michigan just found your uncle guilty. Who decides how long your uncle goes to jail?

options.explanation: The jury's job ended when it decided whether the person on trial did it. Picking the punishment is a separate job at a separate hearing.
The prosecutor can ask for a sentence. Asking for one and deciding it are two different things.
The two sides can agree on what to ask for. The judge still decides what the sentence actually is.

questions.hint: The jury is done. Somebody else does the next part.
questions.principle: In Michigan the judge picks the sentence. The jury does not. Six states let a jury do it, and Texas is one. Michigan is not.

keyPhrase.quote: The jury says whether. The judge says how long.
keyPhrase.gloss: Two jobs, two people.

scenario.setup: Your neighbor's trial finished this morning. The jury said guilty. His family is in the hallway.

lines.label: NEIGHBOR
lines.text: So that's it? It's over?

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: No. The judge does the sentence at a separate hearing.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The family is in the room on the day it actually gets decided.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Everybody goes home thinking it is finished, and nobody turns up.

questions.q: You are on a jury and the room cannot agree on what the law means. What are jurors supposed to do?

options.text: Send the judge a written question.
Go with whichever lawyer explained it better.
options.explanation: Lawyers argue. What a lawyer says about the law is an argument, not the rule the jury has to follow.

options.text: Vote on what the room thinks it means.
options.explanation: A jury applies the law to the facts. Deciding what the law means is not the jury's job.

options.text: Ask the bailiff to explain it.
options.explanation: A bailiff can carry the jury's note to the judge. Explaining the law is not a bailiff's job.

questions.hint: Only one person in the building is allowed to answer that.
questions.principle: The judge hands the jury written instructions. Those explain the law. Jurors decide what happened. The judge decides what the law is. A stuck jury sends the judge a note.

keyPhrase.quote: Jurors decide facts, not law.
keyPhrase.gloss: A stuck jury asks the judge, in writing.

scenario.setup: Your aunt is on a jury and the room cannot agree what the law means.

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Half of them think it means one thing, half the other.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can't you just ask the judge?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: A written question goes out and the same answer comes back to everybody.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The room settles it themselves and the verdict rests on a guess about the law.

questions.q: You are watching a case from the seats and there is no jury in the room. What is a trial like that called?

options.explanation: A trial without a jury is a real trial with a real verdict. No jury is coming.
A trial with no jury is the real trial, not a practice round before one.
A trial with no jury is still open to the public. No jury does not mean closed doors.

questions.hint: The judge is sitting on something called the bench.
questions.principle: A trial with no jury is called a bench trial. The judge does both jobs. The judge decides what happened, and what the law is. Most cases never reach a trial at all.

keyPhrase.quote: No jury means the judge does both jobs.
keyPhrase.gloss: It is called a bench trial.

scenario.setup: Back row of a courtroom with your mom. There is no jury.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Where's the jury? I thought there'd be twelve people.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: There isn't one. The man on trial picked a bench trial, so the judge decides it.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You stay and follow it through to the verdict.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You go looking for the real trial and miss the end of this one.

questions.q: A shoplifting charge against you in Michigan is going to trial with a jury. Which of these does the jury decide?

options.text: How long you go to jail.
options.explanation: In Michigan the judge sets the sentence at a separate hearing after the verdict.
The judge gives the jury the law in writing. The jury applies it.
A jury does not review the decision to charge. That was made long before by the prosecutor.

questions.hint: A jury answers one question, and it is a question about facts.
questions.principle: A jury decides one thing. Was the case proved. Not the sentence. Not what the law means. In Michigan a felony jury has 12 people. A misdemeanor jury has 6.

keyPhrase.quote: One question, and it is about facts.
keyPhrase.gloss: Did it happen, and did this person do it.

scenario.setup: A jury summons came in the post for your uncle.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: I'm not deciding how long somebody goes away for. I'll get out of it.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That part isn't yours. The judge does that.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He turns up knowing what he is actually being asked to decide.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He tries to get excused over a job that was never his.

questions.q: Your cousin has a hearing next week and wants to explain things to the judge before then. When can the judge listen?

options.text: In court, with both sides there.
Any time, in the judge's office.
options.explanation: A private word with the judge about a case is exactly what the rule does not allow.
Going through a lawyer does not make a one-sided conversation allowed. The rule is about who is present, not who is speaking.
The judge does listen. It just has to happen in the open, with both sides there.

questions.hint: The rule is not about when. It is about who else is there.
questions.principle: A judge cannot hear one side alone. It is called ex parte, and it is not allowed. The rule is there so nothing gets decided in secret. You do get heard. It happens in the courtroom.

keyPhrase.quote: Both sides, or neither.
keyPhrase.gloss: A judge cannot listen to one person alone.

scenario.setup: A hearing you are watching. Somebody in the gallery stands up to speak.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: Anything you want me to hear has to be said in here, with both sides present.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So he has to wait?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: It gets said in the hearing, on the record, where it counts.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He keeps trying to catch the judge outside and it never reaches anybody.

questions.q: On the first day of your trial, you realize the judge knows your family from church. What is the judge supposed to do?

options.explanation: Quietly stepping off hides the reason from the people who needed to hear it.
The point is not whether anything went wrong. It is that both sides get to know and can say whether it is a worry.

options.text: Ask your family to stay out of the courtroom.
options.explanation: The connection is what matters, not who is sitting in the seats.

questions.hint: The fix for a judge knowing somebody is not secrecy.
questions.principle: A judge who knows somebody in a case has to say so out loud. Then both sides can object. Sometimes the judge steps aside. Sometimes both sides are fine with it. Either way it happens in the open.

keyPhrase.quote: A judge says it out loud.
keyPhrase.gloss: Connections get disclosed, not hidden.

scenario.setup: A hearing that has not started yet.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: For the record, I know this family from church. Either side may object.

lines.label: LAWYER
lines.text: No objection.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Both sides heard it at the start and the hearing stands.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: It surfaces months later and the whole hearing gets challenged.

questions.q: Your class is watching a trial on a school trip. Which of these is the judge's job?

options.text: Making sure the rules get followed.

options.explanation: A judge does not investigate. Each side builds and brings its own case.

options.text: Making sure guilty people get convicted.
options.explanation: That would make the judge a second prosecutor, which is not what the job is.

options.text: Making sure the prosecutor is fair to the person on trial.
options.explanation: That would make the judge the defense lawyer. The person on trial already has one.

questions.hint: Everybody else in the room has a side. What is left?
questions.principle: A judge runs the process and applies the law. Not on your side. Not on the state's side. Each side builds its own case. One person makes sure it is done by the rules.

keyPhrase.quote: The judge runs the rules, not a side.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everybody else in the room has one.

scenario.setup: School trip. The class is watching a hearing.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: The judge hasn't asked one question about what actually happened.

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: That's not the judge's job. Both lawyers do that part.

scenario.note: The judge runs the rules. The arguing is somebody else's job.

questions.q: You are waiting outside the courtroom for your own hearing when the prosecutor offers to explain what happens next. Who does the prosecutor work for?

options.explanation: A prosecutor is one of the two sides. The neutral person in the room is the judge.
A prosecutor talks to victims and takes a victim's views seriously. The victim is still not the client.
The prosecutor's office is separate from the court, with its own boss and its own budget.

questions.hint: Somebody brought this case. Who was it?
questions.principle: A prosecutor works for the state. That is why cases are called The People against somebody. In Michigan the job title is prosecuting attorney. Most states say district attorney. TV says DA. Same job.

keyPhrase.quote: The prosecutor works for the state.
keyPhrase.gloss: Being friendly is not the same as being on your side.

scenario.setup: The hallway before your neighbor's hearing. The prosecutor comes over.

lines.label: PROSECUTOR
lines.text: Want to tell me your side before we go in?

lines.label: NEIGHBOR
lines.text: I'll wait for my lawyer.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing goes to the other side before his own lawyer hears it.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He explains everything to the person arguing against him.

questions.q: Somebody stole your bike and the case is going to court. What are you in that case?

options.explanation: Being the person it happened to is not the same as bringing the case. The state brings it.
A prosecutor has a client, and the client is the government.

options.text: A party, the same as the defendant.
options.explanation: The two parties are the state and the person charged. The victim is not a party.

questions.hint: Ask whose name the case is brought in.
questions.principle: A crime counts as harm to the whole community. So the state brings the case, not the victim. Victims in Michigan still have real rights, like being told what is happening and speaking at sentencing. Those come from a state law, not from being the client.

keyPhrase.quote: The victim is a witness, not the client.
keyPhrase.gloss: The case belongs to the state.

scenario.setup: Somebody took your bike. A meeting at the prosecutor's office.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So you're my lawyer for this?

lines.label: PROSECUTOR
lines.text: No. I represent the state. You're a witness.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You ask about being told the dates and speaking at sentencing.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You sit back and wait for a lawyer who was never yours.

questions.q: Your cousin was just charged with a crime and wants answers at the courthouse. Which of these people is allowed to give your cousin legal advice?

options.explanation: The prosecutor is the other side of the case. The other side cannot give advice.
A judge decides the case. Giving advice would put the judge on one side.
Court staff can explain what a form is and where it goes. Telling anyone what to do is not allowed.

questions.hint: Advice has to come from somebody whose job is the person charged.
questions.principle: Only your own lawyer can tell you what to do. Court clerks are not allowed to. A clerk will say what a form means. A clerk will not say what to put on it. Clerks work under that rule.

keyPhrase.quote: Advice comes from your side only.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everybody else can explain, not advise.

scenario.setup: The clerk's counter on the first floor.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Should I check this box or not?

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: I can tell you what the box means. I can't tell you what to pick.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You get an actual answer from somebody allowed to give one.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You guess, and the form comes back to be done again.

questions.q: You are watching your uncle's trial when the prosecutor tells the judge something that helps your uncle. Why would the other side do that?

options.text: Because the job is to be fair, not to win.
Because the prosecutor has switched sides.
options.explanation: A prosecutor can be fair to the person on trial and still be the other side. Both are true at once.

options.text: Because the case is about to be dropped.
options.explanation: Saying something fair about the other side does not mean the case is about to end.

options.text: Because the judge made the prosecutor say it.
options.explanation: Saying something to the judge is just how court works. It does not change who a prosecutor represents.

questions.hint: Winning is not the job.
questions.principle: A prosecutor is meant to be fair, not to win at all costs. That means telling the court things that help the other side. Doing the job well can look like being nice. The side has not changed.

keyPhrase.quote: Fair is not the same as friendly.
keyPhrase.gloss: And friendly is not the same as yours.

scenario.setup: Your neighbor's hearing goes better than expected.

lines.label: PROSECUTOR
lines.text: For the record, he's been at every hearing.

lines.label: NEIGHBOR
lines.text: Wait, is she on my side now?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He keeps running everything past his own lawyer.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He starts treating the other side as an ally.

questions.q: The court gave your brother a lawyer because the family cannot pay. Whose side is that lawyer on?

options.explanation: Being appointed by the court does not make the court the client. The client is the person being defended.

options.text: The county's, since the county pays.
options.explanation: Who signs the check and who the client is are two different things.
An appointed lawyer has exactly one client, and it is the person being defended.

questions.hint: Ask who the lawyer has to keep secrets for.
questions.principle: An appointed lawyer is paid by the county and works for the client. Those are two different things. The client gets the same duties as somebody who paid. Loyalty. Secrets kept. A lawyer's best work.

keyPhrase.quote: Paid by the county, working for the client.
keyPhrase.gloss: Who pays is not whose side the lawyer is on.

scenario.setup: The kitchen. Your aunt is explaining the lawyer the court gave your cousin.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: If the county's paying, whose side is she really on?

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: His. That part doesn't change.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The family starts telling the lawyer everything she needs.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Everybody treats her as an outsider and holds things back.

questions.q: A friend tells you a court-appointed lawyer is not a real lawyer. What is a court-appointed lawyer?

options.text: A licensed lawyer, the same as any other.

options.explanation: Appointed lawyers hold a license. Many have done more trials than one you could hire.

options.text: Somebody from the court, not a lawyer.
options.explanation: Appointed counsel is a lawyer with a license who works for you, not somebody employed by the court.

options.text: A lawyer you pick from a list.
options.explanation: You get a lawyer. Michigan courts have said you do not get to pick which one.

questions.hint: One of these is about the lawyer, not how the lawyer was assigned.
questions.principle: An appointed lawyer went to law school and passed the bar. Same license as any other lawyer. Michigan courts have said this: you get a lawyer, but you do not get to pick which one.

keyPhrase.quote: Appointed is how you were assigned, not a kind of lawyer.
keyPhrase.gloss: Same license.

scenario.setup: The bus home from school.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: Public defenders aren't real lawyers though.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: They passed the same bar exam as everybody else.

lines.label: IF HE LISTENS
lines.text: He works with the lawyer the court gives him.

lines.label: IF HE DOESN'T
lines.text: He turns the lawyer down and speaks for himself.

questions.q: You and your appointed lawyer keep disagreeing and you want a different one. What can you do?

options.text: Ask the court, and explain why.
Pick a different one from the county's list.
options.explanation: You do not get to pick an appointed lawyer from a list. The court assigns one.
You can ask the court for a different lawyer when there is a real problem.

options.text: Fire your lawyer the way you would one you paid.
options.explanation: An appointed lawyer is changed through the court, not fired the way a hired lawyer can be.

questions.hint: You can raise it. You cannot go shopping.
questions.principle: Michigan courts have said you get a lawyer, not the lawyer you want. You can ask the court for a different one. You have to give a reason. Not liking the advice is usually not enough. Not being able to work together at all is different.

keyPhrase.quote: You get a lawyer. You do not get to shop.
keyPhrase.gloss: A real problem is worth raising with the court.

scenario.setup: A friend is fed up with the lawyer her family was given.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: We asked for a different one and they just said no.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Did anybody tell the court why?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The actual reason goes to the court and gets looked at.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The family stays unhappy and the judge never hears about it.

questions.q: Your class is watching a criminal trial. Which person in the courtroom argues for the defendant?

options.explanation: The judge runs the rules for both sides and argues for neither.
Family can be there and can speak at sentencing. Family cannot argue the case.
A defendant can choose to go without one, but there is normally a lawyer whose whole job is this.

questions.hint: Everybody in the room has one job. Which one is arguing for the defendant?
questions.principle: One person in that room argues for the defendant. That is the defense lawyer. The judge is neutral. The prosecutor is the other side. Everybody else works for the court.

keyPhrase.quote: One person argues for the defendant.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everybody else has a different job.

scenario.setup: School trip. First time in a courtroom, looking around.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: There's like eight people up there. Which one's for him?

lines.label: TEACHER
lines.text: The one sitting next to him.

scenario.note: One person in that room argues your side. Everybody else has a different job.

questions.q: In Michigan you are charged with a crime that could mean jail time, and there is no money for a lawyer. What happens?

options.text: The court appoints one for you.

options.explanation: Not being able to pay is the reason you get one. Not a reason to go without.

options.text: You get one only if it is a felony.
options.explanation: In Michigan it turns on whether jail is possible, not on whether the charge is labelled a felony.

options.text: Your family has to find the money.
options.explanation: Nobody has to borrow money. That is the entire point of appointed counsel.

questions.hint: This is the criminal side of the courthouse.
questions.principle: Free lawyers are for criminal charges only. In Michigan you get one any time jail is possible. That is more than the law requires. The US Supreme Court set a lower floor. So a state can give less than Michigan does.

keyPhrase.quote: A free lawyer is a criminal-case thing.
keyPhrase.gloss: And only when jail is on the table.

scenario.setup: Your neighbor has court next week and no money for a lawyer.

lines.label: NEIGHBOR
lines.text: I'll just explain it myself. I can't pay anybody.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: If jail's possible they have to appoint one. You have to ask.

lines.label: IF HE ASKS
lines.text: He asks at the first hearing and somebody is appointed.

lines.label: IF HE DOESN'T
lines.text: He goes in alone because he assumed no money meant no lawyer.

questions.q: Your uncle is facing a criminal charge in Michigan and asks the court for a lawyer. What does your uncle have to show?

options.explanation: Whether the crime happened is the whole case. It has nothing to do with getting a lawyer.
The court works out whether jail is possible. Nobody has to argue the stakes.
Nobody has to try hiring a lawyer first. The only question is whether one is affordable.

questions.hint: The word is afford, not innocent.
questions.principle: The test is money. Michigan lists what a court looks at. What you earn. What you own. What you have to pay out. It is usually a short form. Nobody asks what happened.

keyPhrase.quote: The test is money, not guilt.
keyPhrase.gloss: Nobody is asking what happened.

scenario.setup: Filling in a form at the counter before a hearing.

lines.label: NEIGHBOR
lines.text: Does it matter what I'm charged with?

lines.label: CLERK
lines.text: Not on this form. It's asking what you earn.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: The money questions get answered and the lawyer gets appointed.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He writes about the case on a form nobody reads for that, and it goes back.

questions.q: In Michigan, your friend's mom is charged with a crime and cannot afford a lawyer. When is the first chance to ask for one?

options.text: Once a trial date is set.
options.explanation: Most of what matters happens long before a trial date exists.
A lawyer helps most before choices get made, not after.
The court is supposed to ask, and asking yourself is available whether or not anybody offers.

questions.hint: The earliest chance is a real answer here.
questions.principle: Michigan rules say the court has to ask at your first hearing. It has to ask if you want a lawyer and if you can pay. That first hearing is where the charge is read and bond is set. So it matters that somebody is on your side by then.

keyPhrase.quote: The first hearing is the time to ask.
keyPhrase.gloss: The court is supposed to ask you too.

scenario.setup: Your cousin's first appearance. The family is watching.

lines.label: JUDGE
lines.text: Do you want a lawyer, and can you afford one?

lines.label: COUSIN
lines.text: I'll just handle it myself.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He says yes, and somebody is on his side before bond gets set.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The first decisions in the case happen with nobody arguing for him.

questions.q: Nobody is charged with a crime. A store is suing your mom over money it says is owed, and there is no money for a lawyer. What does the court give your mom?

options.text: A free lawyer, the same as in a criminal case.
options.explanation: A lawyer paid for by the court is for criminal charges, not money disputes. Anyone can still hire one.

options.text: A free lawyer if the amount is big enough.
options.explanation: The size of the claim does not switch on a right that is not there in the first place.
The deadline to answer keeps running whether or not you have a lawyer.

questions.hint: Nobody is trying to put anyone in jail here.
questions.principle: There are two systems. A criminal charge means the state wants to punish you. If jail is possible, the court gives you a lawyer. Being sued means somebody wants money. No jail, so the court does not give you one. You can still hire a lawyer. Most people just cannot afford it. More than half of adults think a free one comes with any case. Michigan does appoint lawyers in a few civil cases, like when the state tries to take a child.

keyPhrase.quote: The court only appoints a lawyer for a crime.
keyPhrase.gloss: You can hire one for a money case. Nobody gives you one.

scenario.setup: An envelope on the kitchen table. Somebody is suing your mom over money owed.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: It says 21 days. Do we get a lawyer for this?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Only if we pay for one. The court gives you a lawyer for a crime, not for money.

lines.label: IF SHE ANSWERS
lines.text: She answers in time.

lines.label: IF SHE DOESN'T
lines.text: The deadline passes and the other side wins without a hearing.

questions.q: The prosecutor offers you a plea deal on a theft charge. Your lawyer says take it, and you do not want to. Who decides?

options.explanation: Advice is your lawyer's job. The choice is not.
The judge takes a plea. The judge does not choose it for you.
Your lawyer can disagree out loud and still has to enter what you decided.

questions.hint: Whose case is it?
questions.principle: Michigan rules for lawyers are clear. In a criminal case the lawyer must do what the client decides about three things. The plea. Giving up a jury. Whether to take the stand. Your lawyer's job is making sure you understand the choice.

keyPhrase.quote: The plea is your call.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your lawyer advises. You decide.

scenario.setup: A courtroom drama is on. A lawyer just takes a deal for the client.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can a lawyer even do that?

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Not in real life. That one's the client's call.

scenario.note: The plea belongs to the client, even when the lawyer disagrees out loud.

questions.q: You are watching your cousin's trial, and the defense lawyer skips a question your cousin wanted asked. Who decides how the trial is run?

options.explanation: The big choices belong to the client. How to run the questioning is professional judgment.
The judge rules on objections. The judge does not decide either side's questions.
Paying buys a lawyer, not control of the tactics.

questions.hint: Some calls belong to the client. This is not one of the three.
questions.principle: Three choices belong to the client. The plea, the jury, and whether to take the stand. Which witnesses to call is the lawyer's call. So is what to ask. That split is written into the rules. A question left out may have been left out on purpose. Asking why is fair.

keyPhrase.quote: Three decisions are the client's. The tactics are the lawyer's.
keyPhrase.gloss: A skipped question may have been skipped on purpose.

scenario.setup: A break in the hallway during your friend's brother's trial.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: The lawyer never asked about the messages. My brother told her to.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Ask her why before you decide she forgot.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He gets the reasoning and stays in the loop.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He stops telling his lawyer anything for the rest of the trial.

questions.q: Your aunt's trial is two weeks away. Which of these is your aunt's decision, not the lawyer's?

options.text: Whether to get up and testify.

options.explanation: Which witnesses to call is professional judgment, and it belongs to the lawyer.
What gets asked is tactics. Also the lawyer's.
Nobody picks a judge. Cases get assigned.

questions.hint: There are exactly three decisions on the client's list, and one of these is on it.
questions.principle: Three choices belong to the client. The plea. Giving up a jury. Whether to take the stand. Everything else is the lawyer's call. It works this way in almost every state, because the rule came from the same model.

keyPhrase.quote: Plea, jury, testify.
keyPhrase.gloss: Those three are the client's. The rest is the lawyer's.

scenario.setup: Your neighbor took a plea years ago and still talks about it.

lines.label: NEIGHBOR
lines.text: Everyone told me what to do. In the end it was my signature.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So the lawyer couldn't just decide?

scenario.note: Three decisions belong to the client: the plea, the jury, and whether to testify.

questions.q: You tell your lawyer you want to plead not guilty and your lawyer disagrees. What does your lawyer have to do?

options.text: Enter whichever plea is better for you.
options.explanation: Your lawyer can say so loudly and on the record, and still has to enter the plea you chose.

options.text: Ask the judge to sort it out.
options.explanation: There is nothing to sort out. The rule already says whose call it is.
A lawyer cannot just walk away over it. Leaving a case takes the court's permission.

questions.hint: The rule does not have an exception for when the lawyer disagrees.
questions.principle: The plea is the client's choice, full stop. A lawyer who disagrees should say so clearly and explain why. Then do what the client chose. A lawyer cannot simply walk away over it. Leaving a case takes the court's permission.

keyPhrase.quote: Disagreeing is allowed. Overriding is not.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your lawyer says so, then does what you chose.

scenario.setup: A film on in the background. A lawyer overrules a client on screen.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Can they actually do that?

lines.label: AUNT
lines.text: Not with a plea. That's the client's, even if the lawyer hates it.

scenario.note: A lawyer can disagree on the record and still has to enter the plea the client chose.

questions.q: You tell your lawyer something you have not told anybody. Who can your lawyer tell?

options.text: The judge, if the judge asks.
options.explanation: A judge asking does not unlock it. What a client tells a lawyer is protected, and courts enforce that.

options.text: The prosecutor, when the two sides share evidence.
options.explanation: Sharing evidence between the two sides does not reach conversations between you and your lawyer.

options.text: Your parents, if you are under 18.
options.explanation: Your lawyer's client is you. Being under 18 does not hand your parents the file.

questions.hint: Ask who the lawyer's client is.
questions.principle: What you tell your lawyer stays there. That holds if you are under 18, because the client is you and not your parents. There are a few narrow limits. A lawyer can speak up to stop a crime before it happens. A lawyer cannot help anyone lie in court. A lawyer can answer back if a client says the lawyer did a bad job. A judge or a parent simply asking does not unlock it.

keyPhrase.quote: Your lawyer keeps it.
keyPhrase.gloss: Not the judge, not the prosecutor, not your parents.

scenario.setup: Careers day at school. A defense lawyer is taking questions.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: If someone tells you something, who can you tell?

lines.label: LAWYER
lines.text: Nobody, unless they say so. Not the judge, not the prosecutor, not their parents.

scenario.note: What you tell your own lawyer stays there, including if you are under 18.

questions.q: You call your mom from jail and talk about your case. What is different about that call compared to a meeting with your lawyer?

options.text: The call can be listened to.

options.explanation: The protection covers your lawyer. It does not stretch to family.

options.text: The call is private if you say it is.
options.explanation: Saying a call is private does not make it private.

options.text: Only the parts about the case are protected.
options.explanation: Nothing about the topic makes a call private. Who you are talking to is what matters.

questions.hint: Ask who is on the other end.
questions.principle: Jails record calls. A recorded call can be played later. That is how jails work, not a law. A message usually plays at the start of the call to say so. Calls with your lawyer are treated differently. Nothing else on that phone is private.

keyPhrase.quote: Only lawyer calls are private.
keyPhrase.gloss: Everything else on that phone is recorded.

scenario.setup: A relative is in jail and the family is working out how to call.

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: Every call out of a jail is recorded. Don't get into the case.

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Even to me?

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Nothing about that night ends up on a recording.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: The family's version of events becomes a file somebody can play back.

questions.q: Your cousin's case is still open, and your cousin has talked about it with several people. Which of these conversations stays private?

options.explanation: A probation officer reports to the court. That is the job.

options.text: Talking to a friend about the case.
options.explanation: A friend can be asked about it later, and a friend can answer.
One to one does not mean off the record. The other side is still the other side.

questions.hint: Only one person in this list has a duty to keep your secrets.
questions.principle: Being private is not about the room. It is about who is listening, and what that person's job is. Your lawyer has to keep what you say. A probation officer has to report it. A friend has no duty either way, and can be asked.

keyPhrase.quote: Privacy comes from the person, not the room.
keyPhrase.gloss: Only your lawyer has that duty.

scenario.setup: Two people on a wall outside school.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: You can tell me, I won't say anything.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: My cousin's lawyer said only she has to keep things.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: Your friend is never put in that position.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: Your friend means it, and gets asked anyway.

questions.q: You tell your lawyer you actually did it. What does your lawyer do next?

options.explanation: Confidentiality covers this. It is one of the main reasons the rule exists at all.
Defending somebody who did it is a normal part of the job, not a problem with it.
The plea is your decision. Knowing the truth does not move that.

questions.hint: Think about whose choice the plea is.
questions.principle: A defense lawyer's job is to make the state prove it. Not to decide if you are guilty. What you say stays private either way. There is one limit. Your lawyer cannot help you lie in court. So the truth changes what your lawyer can use. It does not change whose side your lawyer is on.

keyPhrase.quote: Your lawyer keeps working either way.
keyPhrase.gloss: The job is the state's proof, not your guilt.

scenario.setup: A group chat argument about a true crime show.

lines.label: FRIEND
lines.text: His own lawyer knew he did it. That should be illegal.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: That's the job. The state still has to prove it.

scenario.note: A defense lawyer's job is testing the state's proof, not deciding who is guilty.

questions.q: Someone broke into your car. You reported it, and police charged a person for it. Now you want the case dropped. Who decides whether that happens?

options.explanation: The case belongs to the state. Your view is taken seriously and it does not decide.

options.text: The officer who took the report.
options.explanation: An officer investigates. Whether a case continues is not the officer's call.
A judge rules on what is in front of the court. Dropping a case is the prosecutor's move.

questions.hint: Whose case is it, once it has been filed?
questions.principle: Once charges are filed the case belongs to the state. Not to the person it happened to. A prosecutor will usually ask what a victim wants, and often takes it seriously. It is still the prosecutor's choice. A case can go ahead even when the victim asks it to stop.

keyPhrase.quote: The case belongs to the state.
keyPhrase.gloss: Your view counts. It does not decide.

scenario.setup: The kitchen, a week after reporting the stolen bike.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: I don't want to press charges anymore. Can I stop it?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: They said that's the prosecutor's call now.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: You tell the prosecutor what you want, knowing it may go ahead anyway.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: You stop answering the phone and a subpoena turns up instead.

questions.q: In Michigan an officer arrests you and names a charge at the scene. When does that charge become official?

options.text: As soon as the officer says it.
options.explanation: Police ask for a charge. A prosecutor decides what to bring, or whether to bring anything at all.

options.text: When you are booked at the jail.
options.explanation: Booking is paperwork about who is in the building. It does not create a charge.

options.text: When the judge reads it at your first hearing.
options.explanation: The judge reads the charge out. It arrived already decided by somebody else.

questions.hint: Getting arrested and getting charged are two steps.
questions.principle: In Michigan the police ask a prosecutor for a charge. The prosecutor decides what to file, or whether to file at all. So people get arrested and never charged. Others get charged with something else. Police can write tickets for small things. For anything big, the prosecutor decides.

keyPhrase.quote: Arrested and charged are two steps.
keyPhrase.gloss: The charge is real when it gets filed.

scenario.setup: Kitchen table. Your uncle was arrested last night and let go this morning.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: So that's what you're charged with?

lines.label: UNCLE
lines.text: Not yet. A prosecutor still has to decide.

lines.label: YES
lines.text: He waits for the arraignment before deciding anything.

lines.label: NO
lines.text: He tells everyone the wrong charge for three days.

questions.q: In Michigan, how is a county prosecutor chosen?

options.explanation: Michigan votes for county prosecutors. The state does not pick county prosecutors.
Judges decide cases. Judges do not pick who brings them.
Police look into things. Prosecutors charge. The office is separate, and elected.

questions.hint: The person deciding who gets charged is on a ballot.
questions.principle: Every Michigan county votes for its prosecutor, like it votes for a sheriff. The person who decides who gets charged is on a ballot, and can be voted out. Most states elect prosecutors. A few states appoint prosecutors instead. The assistants in that office are hired, not elected.

keyPhrase.quote: Your county votes for its prosecutor.
keyPhrase.gloss: That power sits with somebody on a ballot.

scenario.setup: A sample ballot on the kitchen table before an election.

lines.label: YOU
lines.text: Why is there an election for prosecutor?

lines.label: MOM
lines.text: Because that's the person who decides what gets charged around here.

scenario.note: Every Michigan county elects its prosecutor, the same way it elects a sheriff.
